intro.text: Yumi's calling: a yoki-hijo's day is ruled by ritual, as attendants feed, bathe and dress her and her warden guides her from prayer at the shrine to the place of ritual.
A woman of Torio, also called Chosen, whose title means "girl of commanding primal spirits". By stacking stones with great artistry she summons spirits and binds them into useful tools.

description.text: Tales exist of yoki-hijo who fell in love.

Few in Torio hold more authority than a yoki-hijo, and it is rude to contradict one, even to pay her a compliment. Her role is seen as service: she is waited on so she can serve others. The rituals laid on her, believed to be the spirits' will, have long limited her freedom, though those in the reform movement live more freely.

items.text: Only girls become yoki-hijo, chosen at birth, it is said, by the spirits, with a sign, a shooting star for instance, marking the birth. No more than sixteen live at any one time, and no more than one is chosen in a year.
Reformed yoki-hijo insist on retiring at seventy, but a yoki-hijo keeps her nature for the rest of her life.

Each yoki-hijo has a warden, or kihomaban, as guardian and sponsor. She is traditionally taken from her parents as a baby, so her warden becomes a second parent, though reformed yoki-hijo keep in touch with their families and visit them for a few weeks a year.

The warden teaches her the customs and rites she has to follow and the skills her work needs. She learns to read so she can learn the prayers, may spend months just studying stones for shape, weight and balance, and then learns to build low stacks on a firm base.
Wardens report to superiors who can remove them. Those superiors can also declare a yoki-hijo unfit and punish her, though that is unlikely for one in the reform movement.

A yoki-hijo holds a unique store of power that lets her call the hijo and turn them into tools by binding them. Doing so uses some of it up, but it returns with time and rest. The spirits can hear her thoughts.
Yoki-hijo can also take in or affect raw Investiture.

Almost every part of a traditional yoki-hijo's life is ritual. Besides her warden she has attendants who feed, wash and dress her, though reformed yoki-hijo do some of this themselves and may take days off. Wardens and attendants keep customs of their own, such as set clothing for each day.

In town, the cold spring, or the bath house where there is none, is kept for her alone. Her attendants bathe her with seven soaps on a floating plate, a few for cleaning, such as a red scrubbing powder, most of them perfumed creams. Washes and rinses follow the artist's sequence of progress, from one with the first soap to thirteen with the seventh, and she ends by staying underwater for 144 seconds.
At night her attendants change her into a thin underdress and a heavy formal sleeping gown, and ring her with flower petals and a circle of seeds for luck.

After the morning rituals she goes, screened by fronds, to the town shrine. Of the thirteen ritual prayers, six are essential and take half an hour; she then meditates, about an hour in all, until her warden comes, usually waiting for the local steamwell to erupt before moving on.

She then walks, unscreened so villagers can see her, to the place of ritual, the kimomakkin, usually one to a village and sometimes fenced, where locals have piled stones for her. Villagers gather while spirit scribes sing to chanting, drums and flutes, and she wears kneepads against the hot stone.

Before exhaustion overtakes her she turns to binding. The spirit scribes rank the neediest supplicants, who come forward one by one; she faces a spirit, shares the request and holds a clear picture in her mind, since an unclear one can confuse or scare the spirit away. When every spirit is bound, her attendants take her back to the wagon.

Over several hours she builds dozens of stacks, often of thirty stones or more, though shorter, more intricate ones also work, and feels a tug as the spirits are drawn to them. Most yoki-hijo draw six to ten spirits in a session.
Yoki-hijo travel Torio by wagon, moving at night and visiting a new town each day, to summon the local spirits and bind them into devices the villagers need to survive.
